### 3.4.2 Battery Energy Interaction Graph

#### 3.4.2.1 Motivation

The Dynamic Temporal Multi-Agent Graph introduced in the previous section establishes the battery pack as a graph-structured cyber-physical system. However, representing cells merely as graph nodes and balancing routes as graph edges is insufficient for accurately modeling the complex interactions occurring inside modern lithium-ion battery packs.

A balancing action affects considerably more than the SOC difference between two cells. Each transfer modifies electrical energy distribution, converter loading, thermal generation, degradation trajectories, switching utilization, and future balancing opportunities. Consequently, the battery pack should not be viewed as a simple connectivity graph but as an **energy interaction network**, where every balancing decision induces coupled physical interactions across multiple domains.

To capture these coupled dynamics, we introduce the **Battery Energy Interaction Graph (BEIG)**, a multiplex graph representation that unifies electrical, thermal, degradation, and routing interactions within a common mathematical framework. Unlike conventional graph formulations, the proposed graph serves as the optimization substrate upon which reinforcement learning, combinatorial optimization, and quantum optimization are jointly constructed.

---

#### 3.4.2.2 Multiplex Graph Representation

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph at time $t$ is defined as

$$
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
=
\left(
\mathcal{V},
\mathcal{E}^{elec}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{therm}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{aging}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{route}_t,
\mathbf{W}_t
\right),
$$

where

- $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of battery-cell nodes;
- $\mathcal{E}^{elec}_t$ models electrical energy-transfer feasibility;
- $\mathcal{E}^{therm}_t$ models thermal interaction;
- $\mathcal{E}^{aging}_t$ models degradation coupling;
- $\mathcal{E}^{route}_t$ represents hardware routing feasibility;
- $\mathbf{W}_t$ contains edge weights.

Unlike a conventional graph,

$$
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
\neq
(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})
$$

because multiple interaction layers coexist simultaneously.

The graph may therefore be viewed as

$$
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
=
\bigcup_{k=1}^{4}
\mathcal{G}^{(k)}_t,
$$

where

$$
\mathcal{G}^{(1)}
=
\mathcal{G}^{elec},
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}^{(2)}
=
\mathcal{G}^{therm},
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}^{(3)}
=
\mathcal{G}^{aging},
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}^{(4)}
=
\mathcal{G}^{route}.
$$

Each layer captures a distinct physical mechanism while sharing the same node set.

---

#### 3.4.2.3 Electrical Interaction Layer

The electrical layer models the potential for direct energy transfer between cells.

A directed edge

$$
e^{elec}_{ij}
$$

exists if

$$
SOC_i-SOC_j
>
\Delta_{SOC}^{min}.
$$

The electrical edge weight is defined as

$$
w^{elec}_{ij}
=
\eta_{ij}
\,
\Delta SOC_{ij},
$$

where

$$
\Delta SOC_{ij}
=
SOC_i-SOC_j,
$$

and

$$
\eta_{ij}
$$

denotes converter efficiency.

The electrical adjacency matrix is

$$
A^{elec}
=
[a^{elec}_{ij}],
$$

with

$$
a^{elec}_{ij}
=
\begin{cases}
1,
&
w^{elec}_{ij}>0
\\
0,
&
\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

This layer captures the physical capability of transferring electrical energy.

---

#### 3.4.2.4 Thermal Interaction Layer

Electrical balancing inevitably generates heat. Consequently, balancing routes should not be evaluated solely by their balancing benefit but also by their thermal impact.

The thermal interaction graph associates each edge with the incremental thermal cost resulting from executing that transfer.

The thermal edge weight is defined as

$$
w^{therm}_{ij}
=
\lambda_T
\left(
T_i
+
T_j
\right)
+
\lambda_L
P^{loss}_{ij},
$$

where

$$
P^{loss}_{ij}
=
(1-\eta_{ij})
I_{ij}V_{ij}.
$$

Here,

- $T_i$ and $T_j$ denote source and target temperatures,
- $P^{loss}_{ij}$ is converter loss,
- $\lambda_T$ and $\lambda_L$ are weighting coefficients.

Unlike the electrical layer,

large edge weights are undesirable because they represent increased thermal burden.

---

#### 3.4.2.5 Aging Interaction Layer

Repeated balancing affects battery aging. Aggressive routing through highly degraded cells may accelerate capacity fade and reduce long-term pack performance.

To account for this effect, each edge is assigned an aging interaction weight:

$$
w^{aging}_{ij}
=
\alpha
\left(
1-SOH_i
\right)
+
\beta
\left|
SOH_i-SOH_j
\right|.
$$

The first term penalizes selecting aged source cells, while the second discourages repeated transfers between cells exhibiting significantly different health conditions.

This layer enables degradation-aware balancing policies.

---

#### 3.4.2.6 Routing Interaction Layer

Not every physically meaningful transfer can be executed because balancing hardware imposes switching constraints.

The routing graph models these hardware limitations.

Define

$$
a^{route}_{ij}
=
\begin{cases}
1,
&
\text{converter path exists}
\\
0,
&
\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

The routing weight is

$$
w^{route}_{ij}
=
C^{switch}_{ij}
+
C^{path}_{ij},
$$

where

- $C^{switch}_{ij}$ denotes switching cost,
- $C^{path}_{ij}$ denotes routing complexity.

This layer ensures that the optimization scheduler respects converter topology.

---

#### 3.4.2.7 Unified Edge Weight

The four interaction layers are fused into a single optimization graph.

The unified edge weight is defined as

$$
w_{ij}
=
\omega_1
w^{elec}_{ij}
-
\omega_2
w^{therm}_{ij}
-
\omega_3
w^{aging}_{ij}
-
\omega_4
w^{route}_{ij}.
$$

The positive electrical contribution encourages beneficial balancing, whereas thermal, aging, and routing costs reduce edge desirability.

The coefficient vector

$$
\boldsymbol{\omega}
=
[
\omega_1,
\omega_2,
\omega_3,
\omega_4
]
$$

controls the trade-off among competing objectives and can be tuned or learned.

---

#### 3.4.2.8 Edge Feature Vector

Instead of representing each edge by a scalar weight alone, the proposed framework associates every edge with a rich feature vector:

$$
\mathbf{e}_{ij}
=
\left[
\Delta SOC,
\eta,
P^{loss},
\Delta T,
SOH_i,
SOH_j,
C^{switch},
C^{path}
\right].
$$

The unified weight is then interpreted as

$$
w_{ij}
=
f_{edge}
(\mathbf{e}_{ij}),
$$

where $f_{edge}$ is a deterministic aggregation function in the current work. This abstraction also allows future replacement with learned graph neural edge encoders.

---

#### 3.4.2.9 Graph Fusion

The optimization graph is represented by the weighted adjacency matrix

$$
W_t
=
[w_{ij}]_{N\times N}.
$$

The fused graph is

$$
\mathcal{G}^{opt}_t
=
(\mathcal{V},
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t,
W_t).
$$

Only candidate edges satisfying electrical feasibility, thermal safety, aging limits, and routing constraints remain.

This fused graph becomes the direct input to the scheduler.

---

#### 3.4.2.10 Connection to Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph is shared across all agents.

For agent $i$, the graph neighborhood is

$$
\mathcal{N}_i
=
\{
j
\mid
(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}
\}.
$$

The scheduler provides each agent with the edge feature matrix

$$
\Phi_i
=
\{
\mathbf{e}_{ij}
\mid
j\in\mathcal{N}_i
\}.
$$

Thus, the policy does not observe only neighboring cells but also the physical interaction associated with each candidate route.

This greatly reduces exploration while preserving long-horizon decision capability.

---

#### 3.4.2.11 Bridge Toward Graph Optimization

A key conceptual contribution of the proposed framework is that optimization variables are assigned to graph edges rather than graph nodes.

For every candidate edge,

$$
e_{ij},
$$

define the binary decision variable

$$
x_{ij}
=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if route }(i,j)\text{ is selected},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Collecting all candidate variables yields

$$
\mathbf{x}
=
[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_M]^T,
$$

where $M=|\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t|$.

The optimization objective becomes

$$
\max_{\mathbf{x}}
\sum_{m=1}^{M}
w_m x_m,
$$

subject to routing and safety constraints.

This edge-centric formulation is critical because it converts the battery balancing problem into a binary combinatorial optimization problem.

---

#### 3.4.2.12 Connection to QUBO

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph establishes the mathematical bridge between battery physics and quantum optimization.

Each edge corresponds to a binary optimization variable.

Each interaction between edges induces a quadratic coupling.

The unified optimization objective can therefore be expressed as

$$
E(\mathbf{x})
=
\sum_i
c_i x_i
+
\sum_{i<j}
Q_{ij}x_ix_j,
$$

where

- the linear coefficients $c_i$ are derived from the unified edge weights,
- the quadratic coefficients $Q_{ij}$ arise from conflicts, shared resources, thermal coupling, and scheduling constraints.

Consequently, the Battery Energy Interaction Graph is not merely an intermediate representation. It is the mathematical structure from which the QUBO matrix, Ising Hamiltonian, and quantum optimization formulation naturally emerge.

This graph-centric abstraction enables the proposed framework to unify battery physics, graph theory, combinatorial optimization, quantum optimization, and safe multi-agent reinforcement learning within a single coherent representation.

---

### 3.4.3 Dynamic Temporal Graph

#### 3.4.3.1 Motivation

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph introduced in Section 3.4.2 describes the multi-layer physical interaction structure of a battery pack at a given time step. However, active cell balancing is not performed on a fixed graph. As the battery pack evolves, the graph itself changes. Cell SOC, voltage, temperature, SOH, route feasibility, transfer efficiency, and safety margins are all time-dependent. Consequently, the set of feasible edges, their weights, and the interaction patterns among cells evolve after every load-current update and every balancing action.

This observation motivates the definition of a **Dynamic Temporal Graph** for active cell balancing.

Rather than considering a single static graph,

$$
\mathcal{G}
=
(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{W}),
$$

the proposed framework considers a sequence of time-indexed graphs:

$$
\mathbb{G}_{0:T}
=
\left\{
\mathcal{G}_0,
\mathcal{G}_1,
\dots,
\mathcal{G}_T
\right\}.
$$

Each graph $\mathcal{G}_t$ represents the instantaneous physical and optimization structure of the battery pack at time $t$. The dynamic graph sequence is therefore not merely a record of changing battery states; it is the mathematical object over which sequential balancing decisions are made.

---

#### 3.4.3.2 Temporal Graph Definition

At each discrete time step $t$, the dynamic temporal graph is defined as

$$
\mathcal{G}_t
=
\left(
\mathcal{V},
\mathcal{E}_t,
\mathbf{X}_t,
\mathbf{Z}_t,
\mathbf{W}_t
\right),
$$

where:

$$
\mathcal{V}
=
\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_N\}
$$

is the fixed node set corresponding to battery cells,

$$
\mathcal{E}_t
\subseteq
\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V}
$$

is the time-varying directed edge set,

$$
\mathbf{X}_t
\in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_v}
$$

is the node feature matrix,

$$
\mathbf{Z}_t
\in
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{E}_t|\times d_e}
$$

is the edge feature matrix, and

$$
\mathbf{W}_t
\in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}
$$

is the weighted adjacency matrix.

The node set remains fixed because the physical cells in the pack do not change during an episode. In contrast, the edge set, edge features, and adjacency matrix vary over time according to the digital twin state.

Thus,

$$
\mathcal{V}_{t+1}
=
\mathcal{V}_t
=
\mathcal{V},
$$

but generally,

$$
\mathcal{E}_{t+1}
\ne
\mathcal{E}_t,
$$

$$
\mathbf{W}_{t+1}
\ne
\mathbf{W}_t.
$$

This distinction is important because active balancing changes the optimization problem itself.

---

#### 3.4.3.3 Node Feature Evolution

The feature vector of node $v_i$ at time $t$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{i,t}
=
\left[
SOC_{i,t},
V_{i,t},
T_{i,t},
SOH_{i,t},
R_{0,i},
C_i,
V^{RC}_{i,t},
A_{i,t}
\right],
$$

where $A_{i,t}$ denotes a degradation or aging stress indicator.

The node feature matrix is

$$
\mathbf{X}_t
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_{1,t}^{\top} \\
\mathbf{x}_{2,t}^{\top} \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{x}_{N,t}^{\top}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The node features evolve according to the digital twin transition:

$$
\mathbf{X}_{t+1}
=
F_X
\left(
\mathbf{X}_t,
I^{load}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t,
\Theta
\right).
$$

For example, SOC evolves according to

$$
SOC_{i,t+1}
=
SOC_{i,t}
-
\frac{I_{i,t}\Delta t}
{3600C_i},
$$

temperature evolves according to

$$
T_{i,t+1}
=
T_{i,t}
+
\frac{\Delta t}{C_i^{th}}
\left(
Q^{gen}_{i,t}
-
\frac{T_{i,t}-T_i^{amb}}{R_i^{th}}
\right),
$$

and SOH evolves according to

$$
SOH_{i,t+1}
=
SOH_{i,t}
-
\dot{C}^{aging}_{i,t}\Delta t.
$$

Therefore, the temporal graph is directly coupled to the electrical, thermal, and aging dynamics of the battery digital twin.

---

#### 3.4.3.4 Edge Set Evolution

The edge set $\mathcal{E}_t$ contains directed candidate routes for active balancing. An edge $e_{ij,t}$ exists only when energy transfer from cell $i$ to cell $j$ is physically meaningful and feasible.

The raw physical feasibility condition is

$$
SOC_{i,t}
-
SOC_{j,t}
\ge
\Delta SOC_{min}.
$$

However, SOC difference alone is insufficient. The edge must also satisfy voltage, temperature, SOH, and hardware routing constraints. Thus,

$$
e_{ij,t}
\in
\mathcal{E}_t
$$

if and only if

$$
g_{ij}^{SOC}(s_t)\le 0,
$$

$$
g_{ij}^{V}(s_t)\le 0,
$$

$$
g_{ij}^{T}(s_t)\le 0,
$$

$$
g_{ij}^{SOH}(s_t)\le 0,
$$

$$
g_{ij}^{route}(s_t)\le 0.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\mathcal{E}_t
=
\left\{
(i,j)
\mid
\mathbf{g}_{ij}(s_t)
\le
\mathbf{0},
\quad
i\ne j
\right\}.
$$

Since $s_t$ changes after every transition, $\mathcal{E}_t$ changes dynamically:

$$
\mathcal{E}_{t+1}
=
F_E(s_{t+1}).
$$

This means that balancing decisions alter not only future battery states but also future feasible action sets.

---

#### 3.4.3.5 Temporal Adjacency Matrix

The directed adjacency matrix at time $t$ is

$$
\mathbf{A}_t
=
[a_{ij,t}]
\in
\{0,1\}^{N\times N},
$$

where

$$
a_{ij,t}
=
\begin{cases}
1,
&
(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}_t, \\
0,
&
\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Self-transfer is not allowed:

$$
a_{ii,t}=0,
\quad
\forall i,t.
$$

Because energy transfer is directional,

$$
a_{ij,t}
\ne
a_{ji,t}
$$

in general.

The temporal adjacency sequence is

$$
\mathbf{A}_{0:T}
=
\left\{
\mathbf{A}_0,
\mathbf{A}_1,
\dots,
\mathbf{A}_T
\right\}.
$$

The temporal graph topology can therefore be studied through changes in adjacency:

$$
\Delta \mathbf{A}_t
=
\mathbf{A}_{t+1}
-
\mathbf{A}_t.
$$

A positive entry

$$
\Delta a_{ij,t}=1
$$

indicates that a new feasible route appears at time $t+1$, while

$$
\Delta a_{ij,t}=-1
$$

indicates that a previously feasible route disappears.

This temporal adjacency variation is important because aggressive balancing may remove future balancing opportunities or create new ones.

---

#### 3.4.3.6 Temporal Weighted Graph

The weighted adjacency matrix is

$$
\mathbf{W}_t
=
[w_{ij,t}]
\in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.
$$

If

$$
(i,j)\notin\mathcal{E}_t,
$$

then

$$
w_{ij,t}
=
-\infty
$$

or the edge is masked out.

For feasible edges, the weight is computed as

$$
w_{ij,t}
=
\omega_1 w^{elec}_{ij,t}
-
\omega_2 w^{therm}_{ij,t}
-
\omega_3 w^{aging}_{ij,t}
-
\omega_4 w^{route}_{ij,t}.
$$

The temporal weighted graph is therefore

$$
\mathcal{G}_t^W
=
(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}_t,\mathbf{W}_t).
$$

The weight evolution is written as

$$
\mathbf{W}_{t+1}
=
F_W
\left(
\mathbf{X}_{t+1},
\mathcal{E}_{t+1}
\right).
$$

Because node features evolve under digital twin dynamics, edge weights evolve indirectly through physical battery state transitions.

---

#### 3.4.3.7 Graph Transition Function

The temporal graph evolves according to a graph transition function:

$$
\mathcal{G}_{t+1}
=
\mathcal{F}_G
\left(
\mathcal{G}_t,
I^{load}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t,
\Theta
\right).
$$

This transition can be decomposed as

$$
\mathbf{X}_{t+1}
=
F_X
\left(
\mathbf{X}_t,
I^{load}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t,
\Theta
\right),
$$

$$
\mathcal{E}_{t+1}
=
F_E
\left(
\mathbf{X}_{t+1}
\right),
$$

$$
\mathbf{Z}_{t+1}
=
F_Z
\left(
\mathbf{X}_{t+1},
\mathcal{E}_{t+1}
\right),
$$

$$
\mathbf{W}_{t+1}
=
F_W
\left(
\mathbf{Z}_{t+1}
\right).
$$

Thus,

$$
\mathcal{G}_{t+1}
=
\left(
\mathcal{V},
F_E(\mathbf{X}_{t+1}),
F_X(\cdot),
F_Z(\cdot),
F_W(\cdot)
\right).
$$

This decomposition clarifies that graph dynamics are not arbitrary; they are induced by physical state evolution.

---

#### 3.4.3.8 Temporal Edge Feature Tensor

For all feasible edges, the edge feature vector is

$$
\mathbf{z}_{ij,t}
=
\left[
\Delta SOC_{ij,t},
\eta_{ij,t},
P^{loss}_{ij,t},
\Delta T_{ij,t},
SOH_{i,t},
SOH_{j,t},
C^{switch}_{ij,t},
C^{path}_{ij,t}
\right].
$$

The temporal edge feature tensor is

$$
\mathbf{Z}_{0:T}
=
\left\{
\mathbf{Z}_0,
\mathbf{Z}_1,
\dots,
\mathbf{Z}_T
\right\}.
$$

For dense representation, the edge tensor may be written as

$$
\mathcal{Z}_t
\in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times d_e},
$$

where

$$
\mathcal{Z}_{ij,t}
=
\mathbf{z}_{ij,t}.
$$

Invalid edges are masked using

$$
m_{ij,t}
=
a_{ij,t}.
$$

The masked edge tensor becomes

$$
\tilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{ij,t}
=
m_{ij,t}\mathcal{Z}_{ij,t}.
$$

This representation is especially useful for vectorized GPU implementation, where graph operations are performed as batched tensor operations.

---

#### 3.4.3.9 Temporal Graph for Scheduler-Conditioned MARL

The scheduler-conditioned MARL controller does not act on the full temporal graph directly. Instead, the optimization scheduler extracts candidate subgraphs.

At each time step,

$$
\mathcal{G}^{cand}_t
=
\mathcal{S}_Q(\mathcal{G}_t),
$$

where

$$
\mathcal{G}^{cand}_t
=
(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t,\mathbf{W}^{cand}_t).
$$

For agent $i$, the local candidate neighborhood is

$$
\mathcal{N}^{cand}_{i,t}
=
\left\{
j
\mid
(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t
\right\}.
$$

The agent receives candidate edge features:

$$
\Phi_{i,t}
=
\left\{
\mathbf{z}_{ij,t}
\mid
j\in\mathcal{N}^{cand}_{i,t}
\right\}.
$$

The local observation becomes

$$
o_{i,t}
=
\left[
\mathbf{x}_{i,t},
\mathbf{g}_t,
\Phi_{i,t}
\right],
$$

where $\mathbf{g}_t$ is a global pack summary vector:

$$
\mathbf{g}_t
=
\left[
\overline{SOC}_t,
\sigma^2_{SOC,t},
T^{max}_t,
\overline{SOH}_t
\right].
$$

The policy is therefore conditioned on a time-varying graph neighborhood:

$$
a_{i,t}
\sim
\pi_{\theta}
\left(
a_{i,t}
\mid
o_{i,t},
\mathcal{G}^{cand}_t
\right).
$$

This formulation makes the action space adaptive to the current physical state of the battery pack.

---

#### 3.4.3.10 Temporal Graph and Future Opportunity Cost

One reason active balancing cannot be solved purely greedily is that current actions change future graph topology. A route selected at time $t$ may reduce SOC variance immediately but remove a more beneficial route at time $t+1$.

This can be interpreted as a graph opportunity cost.

Let

$$
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_{t+1|a_t}
$$

denote the future candidate edge set resulting from action $a_t$. The opportunity cost of action $a_t$ may be approximated as

$$
C^{opp}_t(a_t)
=
\Psi
\left(
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t
\right)
-
\Psi
\left(
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_{t+1|a_t}
\right),
$$

where $\Psi(\cdot)$ measures the quality or richness of the candidate graph.

One possible definition is

$$
\Psi
\left(
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t
\right)
=
\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t}
\max(0,w_{ij,t}).
$$

Then,

$$
C^{opp}_t(a_t)
=
\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t}
\max(0,w_{ij,t})
-
\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}_{t+1|a_t}}
\max(0,w_{ij,t+1}).
$$

This term captures how current balancing actions modify future optimization opportunities.

Although this work does not require explicit opportunity-cost optimization in all experiments, the dynamic graph formulation makes such extensions natural.

---

#### 3.4.3.11 Temporal Graph Complexity

The maximum number of directed edges in a fully connected battery graph is

$$
|\mathcal{E}^{all}|
=
N(N-1).
$$

However, the feasible edge set is usually much smaller:

$$
|\mathcal{E}_t|
\le
N(N-1).
$$

The candidate edge set is further reduced by the scheduler:

$$
|\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t|
=
M_t
\ll
N(N-1).
$$

For each time step, the dense temporal graph representation requires

$$
O(N^2)
$$

edge storage, while the sparse candidate graph requires

$$
O(M_t)
$$

storage.

Over a horizon $T$, the dense temporal graph sequence has complexity

$$
O(TN^2),
$$

whereas the scheduler-conditioned sparse representation has complexity

$$
O\left(
\sum_{t=0}^{T}M_t
\right).
$$

Since

$$
M_t
\ll
N^2
$$

in practical settings, the scheduler-conditioned graph significantly reduces the computational burden of downstream reinforcement learning and QUBO construction.

---

#### 3.4.3.12 Temporal Graph Sequence as a Learning Object

The dynamic temporal graph also provides a natural representation for future learning extensions.

Instead of learning only from instantaneous states, a policy may learn from graph histories:

$$
\mathbb{G}_{t-H:t}
=
\left\{
\mathcal{G}_{t-H},
\dots,
\mathcal{G}_{t}
\right\},
$$

where $H$ is the history length.

This enables temporal graph learning:

$$
a_t
\sim
\pi_{\theta}
\left(
a_t
\mid
\mathbb{G}_{t-H:t}
\right).
$$

Possible future architectures include graph recurrent networks, graph transformers, temporal graph attention networks, and graph diffusion models. Although the present work focuses on scheduler-conditioned Safe MAPPO, the proposed dynamic graph representation provides a foundation for these extensions.

---

#### 3.4.3.13 Summary

The Dynamic Temporal Graph formulation extends the Battery Energy Interaction Graph from a static representation to a time-evolving decision structure. In the proposed framework:

$$
s_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{G}_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{G}^{cand}_t
\rightarrow
a_t
\rightarrow
s_{t+1}
\rightarrow
\mathcal{G}_{t+1}.
$$

This temporal graph perspective provides four important advantages.

First, it captures the fact that balancing actions reshape future feasible action spaces.

Second, it connects digital twin dynamics with graph-structured optimization.

Third, it allows scheduler-conditioned MARL to operate on compact, physically meaningful candidate subgraphs.

Fourth, it establishes the foundation for QUBO construction, where temporal graph edges become binary optimization variables and graph interactions become quadratic couplings.

Therefore, the dynamic temporal graph is not merely an auxiliary representation. It is the state-dependent optimization manifold on which active balancing decisions are formulated.

### 3.4.4 Edge Weight Modeling

#### 3.4.4.1 Motivation

The previous sections introduced the Battery Energy Interaction Graph and its dynamic temporal extension. In this representation, each directed edge $e_{ij,t}$ denotes a feasible energy transfer route from source cell $i$ to target cell $j$ at time $t$. However, the existence of an edge alone does not determine whether the corresponding route should be selected. Each edge must be evaluated according to its expected benefit, physical cost, safety risk, degradation impact, and future influence on the balancing process.

Therefore, edge weight modeling is a central component of the proposed framework.

In conventional balancing algorithms, route desirability is often determined by a simple SOC difference:

$$
SOC_{i,t}-SOC_{j,t}.
$$

Although this term captures the immediate balancing potential, it ignores several important physical and operational factors. For example, a route with a large SOC gap may be undesirable if the source cell is already hot, heavily aged, or connected through an inefficient converter path. Similarly, a route with moderate immediate benefit may be valuable if it preserves future balancing opportunities and avoids excessive thermal stress.

This work therefore defines a multi-objective physics-informed edge weight that integrates:

$$
\text{SOC benefit},
\quad
\text{energy transfer efficiency},
\quad
\text{thermal risk},
\quad
\text{aging risk},
\quad
\text{switching cost},
\quad
\text{routing cost},
\quad
\text{future opportunity cost}.
$$

The resulting edge weight becomes the bridge between the physical battery state and the optimization scheduler. In later sections, these edge weights become the linear coefficients of the QUBO objective, while edge-edge interactions become quadratic coupling terms.

---

#### 3.4.4.2 Edge Feature Vector

For every feasible directed edge

$$
e_{ij,t}
\in
\mathcal{E}_t,
$$

we define an edge feature vector

$$
\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ij,t}
=
\left[
\phi^{soc}_{ij,t},
\phi^{eff}_{ij,t},
\phi^{loss}_{ij,t},
\phi^{therm}_{ij,t},
\phi^{aging}_{ij,t},
\phi^{switch}_{ij,t},
\phi^{route}_{ij,t},
\phi^{opp}_{ij,t}
\right].
$$

Each component corresponds to a distinct physical or operational aspect of the transfer route.

The scalar edge score is computed as

$$
w_{ij,t}
=
f_w
\left(
\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ij,t}
\right),
$$

where $f_w(\cdot)$ is a physics-informed aggregation function. In the present work, $f_w$ is defined as a weighted linear combination with normalization, while future work may replace it with a learned graph neural edge encoder.

---

#### 3.4.4.3 SOC Balancing Benefit

The primary purpose of active balancing is to reduce SOC dispersion. Therefore, the first and most important edge feature is the SOC gap between source and target cells:

$$
\Delta SOC_{ij,t}
=
SOC_{i,t}
-
SOC_{j,t}.
$$

A route is physically meaningful only if

$$
\Delta SOC_{ij,t}
\ge
\Delta SOC_{min}.
$$

The normalized SOC benefit is defined as

$$
\phi^{soc}_{ij,t}
=
\frac{
\Delta SOC_{ij,t}
-
\Delta SOC_{min}
}{
\Delta SOC_{max}
-
\Delta SOC_{min}
+
\epsilon
},
$$

where $\epsilon$ is a small numerical constant. The normalization ensures that edge scores remain comparable across operating conditions.

The SOC benefit is positive:

$$
\phi^{soc}_{ij,t}
\ge
0.
$$

A larger value indicates a greater immediate opportunity to reduce imbalance.

---

#### 3.4.4.4 Expected SOC Variance Reduction

Although the SOC gap is intuitive, it does not directly measure the expected reduction in pack-level SOC variance. Therefore, we define a variance-reduction estimate.

Let the SOC vector before transfer be

$$
\mathbf{s}_t^{SOC}
=
[
SOC_{1,t},
SOC_{2,t},
\dots,
SOC_{N,t}
]^\top.
$$

If route $i\rightarrow j$ is executed with balancing SOC transfer magnitude $\delta_{ij,t}$, the approximate post-transfer SOC values are

$$
SOC'_{i,t}
=
SOC_{i,t}
-
\delta_{ij,t},
$$

$$
SOC'_{j,t}
=
SOC_{j,t}
+
\eta_{ij}\delta_{ij,t},
$$

while all other cells remain unchanged except for the common load effect.

The expected variance reduction is

$$
\Delta \sigma^2_{ij,t}
=
\sigma^2_{SOC,t}
-
\sigma^2_{SOC,t|ij}^{+},
$$

where

$$
\sigma^2_{SOC,t|ij}^{+}
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{k=1}^{N}
\left(
SOC'_{k,t}
-
\overline{SOC}'_t
\right)^2.
$$

This term provides a more direct estimate of balancing effectiveness than the raw SOC gap.

Therefore, the SOC-related benefit may be defined as

$$
B^{soc}_{ij,t}
=
\lambda_{\Delta}
\Delta SOC_{ij,t}
+
\lambda_{\sigma}
\Delta \sigma^2_{ij,t}.
$$

Here, $\lambda_{\Delta}$ and $\lambda_{\sigma}$ control the relative importance of local SOC gap and global variance reduction.

---

#### 3.4.4.5 Energy Transfer Efficiency and Loss

Active balancing is beneficial only if the energy transfer is sufficiently efficient. Let $\eta_{ij,t}\in(0,1]$ denote the transfer efficiency from cell $i$ to cell $j$. The useful transferred energy over one time step is approximated by

$$
E^{useful}_{ij,t}
=
\eta_{ij,t}
V_{j,t}
u_{ij,t}
\Delta t,
$$

where $u_{ij,t}$ is the balancing current magnitude.

The source-side extracted energy is

$$
E^{src}_{ij,t}
=
V_{i,t}
u_{ij,t}
\Delta t.
$$

The energy loss is

$$
E^{loss}_{ij,t}
=
E^{src}_{ij,t}
-
E^{useful}_{ij,t}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
E^{loss}_{ij,t}
=
u_{ij,t}\Delta t
\left(
V_{i,t}
-
\eta_{ij,t}V_{j,t}
\right).
$$

A normalized loss feature is defined as

$$
\phi^{loss}_{ij,t}
=
\frac{
E^{loss}_{ij,t}
}{
E^{src}_{ij,t}
+
\epsilon
}.
$$

Lower loss is preferable. Therefore, this term appears as a penalty in the edge weight.

---

#### 3.4.4.6 Thermal Risk

Balancing current and converter loss generate heat. If the source or target cell is already near the thermal limit, executing the transfer may be undesirable even if the SOC benefit is large.

The route-level thermal risk is defined as

$$
R^{therm}_{ij,t}
=
\rho_i T_{i,t}
+
\rho_j T_{j,t}
+
\rho_{\Delta}
|T_{i,t}-T_{j,t}|
+
\rho_L P^{loss}_{ij,t},
$$

where $P^{loss}_{ij,t}$ is the estimated conversion loss power.

The thermal margin of cell $i$ is

$$
M^{T}_{i,t}
=
T_{safe}
-
T_{i,t}.
$$

A normalized thermal penalty is

$$
\phi^{therm}_{ij,t}
=
\max
\left(
0,
\frac{
T_{i,t}-T_{ref}
}{
T_{safe}-T_{ref}+\epsilon
}
\right)
+
\max
\left(
0,
\frac{
T_{j,t}-T_{ref}
}{
T_{safe}-T_{ref}+\epsilon
}
\right)
+
\lambda_L
\frac{
P^{loss}_{ij,t}
}{
P^{loss}_{max}+\epsilon
}.
$$

This term increases as source or target temperatures approach the safety limit.

The thermal feasibility constraint is

$$
T_{i,t}
<
T_{safe},
\quad
T_{j,t}
<
T_{safe}.
$$

However, even below the hard safety boundary, high thermal risk should reduce route desirability. Therefore, thermal risk is included both as a hard safety constraint and as a soft edge-weight penalty.

---

#### 3.4.4.7 Aging Risk

Repeatedly using aged cells as balancing sources may accelerate degradation and reduce pack lifetime. Therefore, the edge model includes a degradation-aware cost.

For route $i\rightarrow j$, the aging risk is defined as

$$
R^{aging}_{ij,t}
=
\alpha_1(1-SOH_{i,t})
+
\alpha_2(1-SOH_{j,t})
+
\alpha_3|SOH_{i,t}-SOH_{j,t}|
+
\alpha_4\dot{C}^{aging}_{ij,t}.
$$

Here, $\dot{C}^{aging}_{ij,t}$ is the incremental aging-rate estimate induced by executing transfer $i\rightarrow j$.

The normalized aging feature is

$$
\phi^{aging}_{ij,t}
=
\frac{
R^{aging}_{ij,t}
}{
R^{aging}_{max}
+
\epsilon
}.
$$

This penalty discourages aggressive balancing routes involving highly degraded cells or routes expected to produce additional aging stress.

---

#### 3.4.4.8 Switching Cost

Active balancing requires switching converter paths. Frequent switching may increase hardware stress, control complexity, and electromagnetic interference. Therefore, switching cost is incorporated into edge weight modeling.

Let

$$
s_{ij,t}
\in
\{0,1\}
$$

denote whether route $i\rightarrow j$ was active at the previous time step. If the route was not active but is selected now, a switching event occurs.

The switching cost is defined as

$$
C^{switch}_{ij,t}
=
\mathbb{1}
[
x_{ij,t-1}=0
\land
x_{ij,t}=1
].
$$

For edge scoring before selection, an estimated switching penalty is

$$
\phi^{switch}_{ij,t}
=
1
-
x_{ij,t-1}.
$$

This formulation encourages temporal smoothness by preferring routes that were recently active when such routes remain beneficial and safe.

---

#### 3.4.4.9 Routing Cost

The physical balancing topology may impose different costs for different transfer routes. For example, neighboring-cell transfers may be easier than long-distance transfers depending on converter architecture.

Let $d_{ij}$ denote the routing distance or path complexity between cells $i$ and $j$. The routing cost is defined as

$$
C^{route}_{ij}
=
\lambda_d d_{ij}
+
\lambda_p C^{path}_{ij},
$$

where $C^{path}_{ij}$ captures converter-path complexity.

The normalized routing feature is

$$
\phi^{route}_{ij,t}
=
\frac{
C^{route}_{ij}
}{
C^{route}_{max}
+
\epsilon
}.
$$

This term is especially useful when the balancing topology is not fully connected. In a fully connected abstraction, $C^{route}_{ij}$ may be set to a constant or omitted.

---

#### 3.4.4.10 Future Opportunity Cost

A balancing action changes future graph topology. Selecting an edge with high immediate benefit may reduce future balancing flexibility. Therefore, we introduce a future opportunity-cost term.

Let

$$
\Psi(\mathcal{G}_t)
$$

denote the total positive balancing potential of the current graph:

$$
\Psi(\mathcal{G}_t)
=
\sum_{(k,l)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t}
\max(0,w^{raw}_{kl,t}),
$$

where $w^{raw}_{kl,t}$ is the pre-penalty route benefit.

If route $i\rightarrow j$ is executed, the digital twin predicts a one-step future graph

$$
\mathcal{G}_{t+1|ij}.
$$

The opportunity cost is then

$$
C^{opp}_{ij,t}
=
\Psi(\mathcal{G}_t)
-
\Psi(\mathcal{G}_{t+1|ij}).
$$

A large positive value indicates that executing the route significantly reduces future balancing opportunities.

The normalized opportunity feature is

$$
\phi^{opp}_{ij,t}
=
\frac{
C^{opp}_{ij,t}
}{
C^{opp}_{max}
+
\epsilon
}.
$$

In the current implementation, this term may be approximated using local SOC changes rather than full graph rollout to reduce computational cost.

---

#### 3.4.4.11 Unified Physics-Informed Edge Score

Combining the above terms, the proposed edge score is

$$
w_{ij,t}
=
\lambda_{soc}B^{soc}_{ij,t}
+
\lambda_{eff}\eta_{ij,t}
-
\lambda_{loss}\phi^{loss}_{ij,t}
-
\lambda_{therm}\phi^{therm}_{ij,t}
-
\lambda_{aging}\phi^{aging}_{ij,t}
-
\lambda_{switch}\phi^{switch}_{ij,t}
-
\lambda_{route}\phi^{route}_{ij,t}
-
\lambda_{opp}\phi^{opp}_{ij,t}.
$$

The first two terms reward beneficial and efficient energy transfer. The remaining terms penalize energy loss, thermal risk, aging stress, switching effort, routing complexity, and future opportunity loss.

The coefficient vector is

$$
\boldsymbol{\lambda}
=
[
\lambda_{soc},
\lambda_{eff},
\lambda_{loss},
\lambda_{therm},
\lambda_{aging},
\lambda_{switch},
\lambda_{route},
\lambda_{opp}
].
$$

This vector controls the trade-off among competing objectives. It may be selected manually, tuned through validation, or adapted through meta-learning in future work.

A feasible edge with a larger $w_{ij,t}$ is considered more desirable.

---

#### 3.4.4.12 Cost Form for Optimization

Since QUBO is generally formulated as a minimization problem, the edge score is converted into an edge cost:

$$
c_{ij,t}
=
-w_{ij,t}.
$$

Therefore, selecting a highly desirable edge reduces the total objective value.

For all candidate edges

$$
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t
=
\{
e_1,e_2,\dots,e_M
\},
$$

the linear cost vector is

$$
\mathbf{c}_t
=
[
c_{1,t},
c_{2,t},
\dots,
c_{M,t}
]^\top.
$$

Each component corresponds to one binary edge-selection variable:

$$
x_{m,t}
=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if candidate edge }e_m\text{ is selected},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

The linear part of the QUBO objective becomes

$$
E^{linear}_t(\mathbf{x})
=
\sum_{m=1}^{M}
c_{m,t}x_{m,t}.
$$

Thus, the edge-weight model directly determines the linear coefficients of the QUBO scheduler.

---

#### 3.4.4.13 Edge Weight Normalization

Because different physical quantities have different units and scales, normalization is essential. Without normalization, terms such as temperature, energy loss, and SOC gap may dominate the objective unevenly.

Each feature is normalized as

$$
\tilde{\phi}^{k}_{ij,t}
=
\frac{
\phi^{k}_{ij,t}
-
\mu_k
}{
\sigma_k+\epsilon
},
$$

or alternatively,

$$
\tilde{\phi}^{k}_{ij,t}
=
\frac{
\phi^{k}_{ij,t}
-
\phi^{k}_{min}
}{
\phi^{k}_{max}
-
\phi^{k}_{min}
+
\epsilon
}.
$$

The normalized edge score is

$$
w_{ij,t}
=
\sum_{k}
\lambda_k
\tilde{\phi}^{k}_{ij,t}.
$$

For stability, the final weight may be clipped:

$$
w_{ij,t}
\leftarrow
\text{clip}
(w_{ij,t},w_{min},w_{max}).
$$

This improves numerical stability for both classical solvers and QUBO-to-Ising transformations.

---

#### 3.4.4.14 Edge Masking

Not every edge with a computed score should remain available. Edge masking ensures that infeasible routes are excluded before optimization.

The binary feasibility mask is

$$
m_{ij,t}
=
\mathbb{1}
[
e_{ij,t}
\in
\mathcal{E}^{safe}_t
].
$$

The masked edge score is

$$
\hat{w}_{ij,t}
=
m_{ij,t}w_{ij,t}
+
(1-m_{ij,t})(-\infty).
$$

Equivalently, infeasible edges are removed from the candidate set:

$$
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t
=
\{
(i,j)
\mid
m_{ij,t}=1
\}.
$$

The mask is determined by hard constraints, including:

$$
SOC_{i,t}-SOC_{j,t}
\ge
\Delta SOC_{min},
$$

$$
SOC_{i,t}-\delta_{ij,t}
\ge
SOC_{min},
$$

$$
SOC_{j,t}+\eta_{ij}\delta_{ij,t}
\le
SOC_{max},
$$

$$
V_{min}
\le
V_{i,t},V_{j,t}
\le
V_{max},
$$

$$
T_{i,t},T_{j,t}
\le
T_{safe}.
$$

Thus, unsafe edges are excluded before QUBO construction and before MARL action selection.

---

#### 3.4.4.15 Edge Weight Matrix

The complete edge weight matrix is

$$
\mathbf{W}_t
=
[w_{ij,t}]
\in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.
$$

Since the graph is directed,

$$
w_{ij,t}
\ne
w_{ji,t}
$$

in general.

Self-transfer is invalid:

$$
w_{ii,t}
=
-\infty.
$$

The masked weighted adjacency matrix is

$$
\hat{\mathbf{W}}_t
=
\mathbf{M}_t
\odot
\mathbf{W}_t,
$$

where $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication and $\mathbf{M}_t$ is the feasibility mask.

For implementation, infeasible entries may be assigned a large negative value rather than $-\infty$:

$$
\hat{w}_{ij,t}
=
\begin{cases}
w_{ij,t},&m_{ij,t}=1,\\
-\kappa,&m_{ij,t}=0,
\end{cases}
$$

where $\kappa\gg 0$.

---

#### 3.4.4.16 Interpretation for Reinforcement Learning

For the MARL controller, the edge weight plays two roles.

First, it provides candidate ranking. The scheduler selects the top $K$ outgoing candidate edges for each agent based on $w_{ij,t}$. Thus, each cell-agent receives a compact local action set.

Second, it provides physically meaningful edge features. The agent does not need to infer the value of a route only from raw cell states. Instead, it observes route-level information such as SOC benefit, thermal risk, aging risk, and efficiency.

The candidate set for agent $i$ is

$$
\mathcal{N}^{cand}_{i,t}
=
\text{TopK}
\left(
\{
j
\mid
(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{safe}_t
\},
w_{ij,t}
\right).
$$

The agent observation includes

$$
\Phi_{i,t}
=
\{
\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ij,t},
w_{ij,t}
\mid
j\in\mathcal{N}^{cand}_{i,t}
\}.
$$

Thus, the learning policy operates on scheduler-filtered, physics-informed, graph-structured actions.

---

#### 3.4.4.17 Interpretation for QUBO

For the QUBO scheduler, each candidate edge corresponds to a binary variable. The edge cost is

$$
c_m=-w_m.
$$

The QUBO linear term is

$$
\sum_{m=1}^{M}c_m x_m.
$$

If edge $m$ has high balancing value, then $w_m$ is large and $c_m$ becomes strongly negative. Minimizing the QUBO therefore encourages selecting the edge.

However, selecting multiple individually valuable edges may create conflicts. These conflicts are captured by quadratic terms:

$$
\sum_{m<n}Q_{mn}x_mx_n.
$$

Therefore, the edge weight model provides the first half of the QUBO construction:

$$
\text{edge value}
\rightarrow
\text{linear QUBO coefficient}.
$$

The next step is to model edge-edge interactions, which generate the quadratic coefficients.

---

#### 3.4.4.18 Summary

The proposed edge weight model transforms raw battery states into physically meaningful optimization coefficients. Unlike simple SOC-gap-based balancing rules, the proposed edge score integrates immediate balancing benefit, energy efficiency, thermal risk, degradation cost, switching cost, routing complexity, and future opportunity cost.

This modeling choice is essential for three reasons.

First, it allows the scheduler to evaluate balancing routes using multi-objective physical criteria.

Second, it provides the MARL controller with informative candidate route features, reducing exploration burden.

Third, it directly maps battery physics into the linear coefficients of the QUBO objective.

Therefore, edge weight modeling is the key mathematical interface between the dynamic graph representation and the quantum-compatible optimization scheduler.

# 왜 Conflict Graph가 중요한가?

우리가 지금까지 만든 것은

```text
Node

↓

Edge

↓

Edge Weight
```

입니다.

하지만 QUBO는

```text
Edge

↓

Edge 와 Edge 의 관계
```

를 모델링합니다.

즉

QUBO는

Node가 아니라

**Edge들의 충돌(Conflict)** 을 최적화합니다.

---

예를 들어

```text
1 → 4

2 → 4
```

두 Edge가 있습니다.

둘 다 좋아 보입니다.

하지만

동시에 실행할 수 없습니다.

왜냐하면

Cell4는

동시에

두 개의 에너지를 받을 수 없기 때문입니다.

---

또

```text
5 → 2

5 → 7
```

도 안 됩니다.

Source Cell은

동시에

두 군데로 에너지를 줄 수 없습니다.

---

또

```text
3 → 5

5 → 9
```

도

동시에 하면

Scheduling conflict가 생길 수도 있습니다.

---

즉

Conflict는

Node에서 발생하는 것이 아니라

**Edge들끼리 발생합니다.**

이게 핵심입니다.

---

# 그래서

저는 여기서

새로운 Graph를 정의하려고 합니다.

Battery Graph가 아니라

## Conflict Graph

입니다.

---

Battery Graph

```text
Node = Cell

Edge = Transfer
```

---

Conflict Graph

```text
Node = Transfer Edge

Edge = Conflict
```

이게 엄청 중요합니다.

---

예를 들어

Battery Graph

```text
1 → 5

3 → 7

8 → 2
```

에서는

Node가

Cell입니다.

하지만

Conflict Graph에서는

Node가

```text
(1→5)

(3→7)

(8→2)
```

입니다.

그리고

Conflict가 있으면

Node끼리 연결합니다.

QUBO Matrix가

자동으로 나옵니다.

왜냐하면

Conflict가 있는 두 Edge는

동시에

선택하면 안 되기 때문입니다.

즉

Quadratic Penalty

$$
Q_{ij}x_ix_j
$$

가

바로

Conflict Edge입니다.

### 3.4.5 Conflict Graph

#### 3.4.5.1 Motivation

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph developed in the previous sections models feasible energy-transfer routes as directed edges connecting battery cells. Each edge is associated with a physics-informed weight representing the expected benefit and cost of executing that transfer. However, selecting the highest-scoring edges independently does not necessarily produce a feasible balancing schedule.

The fundamental reason is that balancing routes are not independent. Multiple candidate routes may compete for the same battery cell, the same converter, the same switching path, or the same thermal margin. Consequently, selecting one route may invalidate another even if both routes are individually beneficial.

This dependency cannot be represented by node or edge weights alone.

Instead, the dependency must be modeled as **interactions between edge-selection variables**.

To capture these interactions, we introduce the **Conflict Graph**, a higher-order graph in which nodes represent candidate balancing routes and edges represent conflicts between those routes.

Unlike the Battery Energy Interaction Graph, whose nodes correspond to physical battery cells, the Conflict Graph operates in the optimization domain. It describes relationships among decision variables rather than relationships among physical components.

This graph provides the mathematical foundation for constructing the quadratic interaction terms of the QUBO formulation.

---

#### 3.4.5.2 Edge-Centric Optimization Space

Let

$$
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t
=
\{e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_M\}
$$

be the candidate balancing routes generated by the scheduler.

Each candidate edge

$$
e_m
=
(i,j)
$$

corresponds to a binary optimization variable

$$
x_m
=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if route }e_m\text{ is selected},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Unlike the Battery Energy Interaction Graph, where nodes represent battery cells, the Conflict Graph defines each candidate edge as a graph node:

$$
\mathcal{V}^{conf}
=
\{
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_M
\}.
$$

The edge set of the Conflict Graph is

$$
\mathcal{E}^{conf}
=
\{
(x_m,x_n)
\mid
x_m
\text{ conflicts with }
x_n
\}.
$$

Thus,

$$
\mathcal{G}^{conf}
=
(
\mathcal{V}^{conf},
\mathcal{E}^{conf},
\mathbf{C}
),
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{C}
=
[c_{mn}]
$$

is the conflict matrix.

Unlike the weighted adjacency matrix of the Battery Energy Interaction Graph, the conflict matrix measures incompatibility between balancing routes.

---

#### 3.4.5.3 Source Conflict

A source conflict occurs when one battery cell attempts to transfer energy simultaneously to multiple destination cells.

Suppose

$$
e_m=(i,j),
$$

and

$$
e_n=(i,k),
$$

where

$$
j\neq k.
$$

Both routes originate from the same source cell.

Executing both routes simultaneously would require the source cell to deliver energy to multiple destinations during the same balancing interval.

Such an operation is not allowed under the assumed balancing hardware.

Therefore,

$$
c^{src}_{mn}
=
1.
$$

Formally,

$$
c^{src}_{mn}
=
\mathbb{1}
[
i_m=i_n
].
$$

The corresponding quadratic penalty is

$$
P_{src}
=
\lambda_{src}
\sum_{m<n}
c^{src}_{mn}
x_mx_n.
$$

The penalty guarantees that at most one outgoing balancing route is selected for each source cell.

---

#### 3.4.5.4 Destination Conflict

Similarly, two balancing routes cannot simultaneously terminate at the same destination cell.

Suppose

$$
e_m=(i,j),
$$

and

$$
e_n=(k,j).
$$

Both routes attempt to charge cell

$$
j.
$$

The destination conflict indicator is

$$
c^{dst}_{mn}
=
\mathbb{1}
[
j_m=j_n
].
$$

The corresponding quadratic penalty becomes

$$
P_{dst}
=
\lambda_{dst}
\sum_{m<n}
c^{dst}_{mn}
x_mx_n.
$$

This prevents multiple sources from charging the same destination during the same balancing interval.

---

#### 3.4.5.5 Cycle Conflict

Another important interaction arises from cyclic energy transfers.

Consider

$$
e_m=(i,j),
$$

and

$$
e_n=(j,i).
$$

Executing both routes simultaneously creates an immediate two-node energy cycle.

Although such cycles may appear mathematically feasible, they produce unnecessary switching activity and converter losses without improving pack balance.

The cycle conflict indicator is

$$
c^{cyc}_{mn}
=
\mathbb{1}
[
i_m=j_n
\land
j_m=i_n
].
$$

The corresponding penalty is

$$
P_{cyc}
=
\lambda_{cyc}
\sum_{m<n}
c^{cyc}_{mn}
x_mx_n.
$$

This formulation naturally extends to longer cyclic structures.

For example,

$$
1\rightarrow2,
$$

$$
2\rightarrow3,
$$

$$
3\rightarrow1
$$

forms a three-node cycle.

Cycle detection may therefore be generalized through graph traversal algorithms.

---

#### 3.4.5.6 Thermal Conflict

Even if two routes involve different cells, they may still compete for the same thermal budget.

Suppose two balancing routes operate inside the same thermal region.

The thermal interaction between two routes is approximated as

$$
R^{therm}_{mn}
=
\exp
\left(
-
\frac{
d^{phys}_{mn}
}
{\sigma_T}
\right),
$$

where

$$
d^{phys}_{mn}
$$

denotes physical distance between the affected cell groups.

Alternatively,

thermal coupling may be obtained directly from the digital twin thermal model.

The thermal conflict coefficient becomes

$$
c^{therm}_{mn}
=
\frac{
R^{therm}_{mn}
}
{
R^{therm}_{max}
}.
$$

Unlike source conflict,

thermal conflict is continuous rather than binary.

Its penalty becomes

$$
P_{therm}
=
\lambda_{therm}
\sum_{m<n}
c^{therm}_{mn}
x_mx_n.
$$

This discourages simultaneous execution of routes producing excessive localized heating.

---

#### 3.4.5.7 Converter Resource Conflict

Many practical balancing circuits contain limited converter resources.

Suppose two candidate routes require the same converter module.

Define

$$
r_m
$$

as the converter assigned to route

$$
e_m.
$$

Then

$$
c^{res}_{mn}
=
\mathbb{1}
[
r_m=r_n
].
$$

The resource penalty is

$$
P_{res}
=
\lambda_{res}
\sum_{m<n}
c^{res}_{mn}
x_mx_n.
$$

This formulation allows the scheduler to enforce hardware utilization constraints without explicitly modeling switching sequences.

---

#### 3.4.5.8 Conflict Matrix

The individual conflict types are combined into a unified conflict matrix:

$$
\mathbf{C}
=
\lambda_{src}\mathbf{C}^{src}
+
\lambda_{dst}\mathbf{C}^{dst}
+
\lambda_{cyc}\mathbf{C}^{cyc}
+
\lambda_{therm}\mathbf{C}^{therm}
+
\lambda_{res}\mathbf{C}^{res}.
$$

Each matrix is symmetric,

$$
\mathbf{C}
=
\mathbf{C}^{\top},
$$

and satisfies

$$
c_{mm}=0.
$$

Each element

$$
c_{mn}
$$

represents the degree of incompatibility between candidate routes

$$
e_m
$$

and

$$
e_n.
$$

This matrix is central to the subsequent QUBO construction.

---

#### 3.4.5.9 Graph Interpretation

Unlike the Battery Energy Interaction Graph,

whose nodes are battery cells,

the Conflict Graph contains optimization variables.

Battery graph:

```text
Cell1 ─────► Cell5

Cell3 ─────► Cell8

Cell4 ─────► Cell2
```

Conflict graph:

```text
(1→5)

│

├──────── (3→5)

│

└──────── (1→8)
```

Thus,

the Conflict Graph represents interactions between balancing decisions rather than interactions between battery cells.

---

#### 3.4.5.10 Quadratic Energy Interpretation

The edge-selection vector is

$$
\mathbf{x}
=
[
x_1,
x_2,
\dots,
x_M
]^{\top}.
$$

The total conflict energy is

$$
E_{conf}
=
\mathbf{x}^{\top}
\mathbf{C}
\mathbf{x}.
$$

Expanding,

$$
E_{conf}
=
\sum_{m<n}
c_{mn}
x_mx_n.
$$

This quadratic interaction energy measures the incompatibility of simultaneously selected balancing routes.

Minimizing this energy naturally eliminates conflicting route combinations.

---

#### 3.4.5.11 Connection to QUBO

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph provides the linear coefficients

$$
\mathbf{c},
$$

while the Conflict Graph provides the quadratic interaction matrix

$$
\mathbf{C}.
$$

Therefore,

the optimization objective becomes

$$
E(\mathbf{x})
=
\mathbf{c}^{\top}\mathbf{x}
+
\mathbf{x}^{\top}
\mathbf{C}
\mathbf{x}.
$$

This expression is already in the canonical form of a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization problem.

No additional reformulation is required.

Consequently,

the Conflict Graph serves as the mathematical bridge between graph optimization and quantum-compatible optimization.

---

#### 3.4.5.12 Discussion

The introduction of the Conflict Graph constitutes one of the central conceptual contributions of this work.

Instead of treating balancing routes as independent optimization variables, the proposed framework explicitly models interactions among decisions. Source conflicts, destination conflicts, cyclic transfers, thermal coupling, and shared converter resources are all represented within a unified quadratic interaction graph.

This representation has three important advantages.

First, it captures the true combinatorial nature of active balancing, where route feasibility depends on interactions among multiple decisions rather than individual route quality.

Second, it naturally supports scheduler-conditioned Safe MARL. The scheduler can eliminate highly conflicting candidates before policy execution, while the policy focuses on long-horizon decision making within a physically feasible action space.

Third, the Conflict Graph directly yields the quadratic coupling matrix required by QUBO, Ising Hamiltonian construction, and future quantum optimization algorithms. In this sense, the Conflict Graph is the missing mathematical layer that connects battery physics with quantum-compatible combinatorial optimization.

---

### 3.4.6 Agent Communication Graph

#### 3.4.6.1 Motivation

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph represents physical energy-transfer opportunities, while the Conflict Graph represents incompatibilities among balancing-route decisions. However, safe multi-agent reinforcement learning requires one additional graph structure: a graph that defines how cell-level agents exchange decision-relevant information.

In the proposed framework, each battery cell is modeled as one cooperative agent. Although each agent observes its own local cell state, balancing decisions are not purely local. A cell deciding whether to transfer energy must consider neighboring SOC levels, candidate transfer routes, local thermal risk, routing conflicts, and pack-level balancing objectives. Therefore, the learning architecture requires a communication structure that determines which agents influence one another during policy execution and centralized training.

This motivates the definition of the **Agent Communication Graph (ACG)**.

The Agent Communication Graph is not necessarily identical to the physical balancing graph. Two cells may need to communicate even if no direct energy-transfer route exists between them. Conversely, two cells may have a feasible transfer path but may not require direct policy-level communication if their decisions are already mediated by the scheduler. Therefore, the communication graph represents decision dependency rather than physical connectivity.

---

#### 3.4.6.2 Definition of the Agent Communication Graph

At time $t$, the Agent Communication Graph is defined as

$$
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t
=
\left(
\mathcal{V}^{agent},
\mathcal{E}^{comm}_t,
\mathbf{H}_t,
\mathbf{A}^{comm}_t
\right),
$$

where

$$
\mathcal{V}^{agent}
=
\{1,2,\dots,N\}
$$

is the set of cell agents,

$$
\mathcal{E}^{comm}_t
\subseteq
\mathcal{V}^{agent}
\times
\mathcal{V}^{agent}
$$

is the communication edge set,

$$
\mathbf{H}_t
=
[
\mathbf{h}_{1,t},
\mathbf{h}_{2,t},
\dots,
\mathbf{h}_{N,t}
]^{\top}
$$

is the agent feature matrix, and

$$
\mathbf{A}^{comm}_t
=
[a^{comm}_{ij,t}]
$$

is the communication adjacency matrix.

Each agent feature vector is defined as

$$
\mathbf{h}_{i,t}
=
\left[
SOC_{i,t},
V_{i,t},
T_{i,t},
SOH_{i,t},
d^{out}_{i,t},
d^{in}_{i,t},
r^{conf}_{i,t},
q_{i,t}
\right],
$$

where $d^{out}_{i,t}$ is the number of feasible outgoing balancing routes, $d^{in}_{i,t}$ is the number of feasible incoming routes, $r^{conf}_{i,t}$ is an agent-level conflict risk score, and $q_{i,t}$ is the scheduler-provided local route quality score.

---

#### 3.4.6.3 Communication Edge Construction

A communication edge between agents $i$ and $j$ may be created according to several dependency criteria.

First, two agents communicate if a feasible energy-transfer route exists between them:

$$
(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{comm}_t
\quad
\text{if}
\quad
(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t
\quad
\text{or}
\quad
(j,i)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t.
$$

Second, agents communicate if their candidate routes conflict in the Conflict Graph. For example, if agent $i$'s outgoing route and agent $j$'s outgoing route compete for the same target cell, the two agents should exchange information or be coupled through centralized coordination.

Let

$$
\Gamma(i)
$$

denote the set of candidate edge variables controlled by agent $i$. Then a conflict-induced communication edge exists if

$$
\exists x_m\in\Gamma(i),\,
\exists x_n\in\Gamma(j)
\quad
\text{such that}
\quad
c_{mn}>0.
$$

Third, thermal proximity may induce communication. If cells $i$ and $j$ belong to the same thermal region or have strong thermal coupling,

$$
\kappa^{therm}_{ij,t}
>
\kappa^{therm}_{min},
$$

then

$$
(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{comm}_t.
$$

Combining these criteria, the communication adjacency is defined as

$$
a^{comm}_{ij,t}
=
\mathbb{1}
[
a^{bal}_{ij,t}
\lor
a^{conf}_{ij,t}
\lor
a^{therm}_{ij,t}
].
$$

Thus, the communication graph fuses physical, optimization, and safety-induced dependencies.

---

#### 3.4.6.4 Communication Weight

The communication edge weight measures the strength of decision dependency between agents.

We define

$$
b_{ij,t}^{comm}
=
\mu_1 b^{bal}_{ij,t}
+
\mu_2 b^{conf}_{ij,t}
+
\mu_3 b^{therm}_{ij,t}
+
\mu_4 b^{soc}_{ij,t}.
$$

The balancing dependency term is

$$
b^{bal}_{ij,t}
=
\mathbb{1}
[
(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t
\lor
(j,i)\in\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t
].
$$

The conflict dependency term is

$$
b^{conf}_{ij,t}
=
\sum_{x_m\in\Gamma(i)}
\sum_{x_n\in\Gamma(j)}
c_{mn}.
$$

The thermal dependency term may be expressed as

$$
b^{therm}_{ij,t}
=
\exp
\left(
-
\frac{d^{phys}_{ij}}{\sigma_T}
\right),
$$

where $d^{phys}_{ij}$ is the physical distance between cells and $\sigma_T$ controls thermal coupling decay.

The SOC dependency term is

$$
b^{soc}_{ij,t}
=
|SOC_{i,t}-SOC_{j,t}|.
$$

The complete communication weight matrix is

$$
\mathbf{B}^{comm}_t
=
[b^{comm}_{ij,t}]
\in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.
$$

This matrix determines how strongly each agent should account for other agents during message aggregation or centralized value estimation.

---

#### 3.4.6.5 Relation to Local Agent Observation

The local observation of agent $i$ was previously defined as

$$
o_{i,t}
=
\left[
\mathbf{x}_{i,t},
\mathbf{g}_t,
\Phi_{i,t}
\right],
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{i,t}$ is the local cell state, $\mathbf{g}_t$ is a global pack summary, and $\Phi_{i,t}$ contains scheduler-provided candidate edge features.

The Agent Communication Graph extends this observation with neighborhood information:

$$
\tilde{o}_{i,t}
=
\left[
o_{i,t},
\mathbf{m}_{i,t}
\right],
$$

where $\mathbf{m}_{i,t}$ is the aggregated message from neighboring agents.

The neighborhood of agent $i$ is

$$
\mathcal{N}^{comm}_{i,t}
=
\{
j
\mid
(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{comm}_t
\}.
$$

A general message aggregation function is

$$
\mathbf{m}_{i,t}
=
\text{AGG}
\left(
\{
b^{comm}_{ij,t}
\psi(\mathbf{h}_{j,t})
\mid
j\in\mathcal{N}^{comm}_{i,t}
\}
\right),
$$

where $\psi(\cdot)$ is an embedding function and AGG may be a weighted sum, mean aggregation, attention pooling, or graph neural message passing.

A simple weighted aggregation is

$$
\mathbf{m}_{i,t}
=
\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}^{comm}_{i,t}}
\alpha_{ij,t}
\psi(\mathbf{h}_{j,t}),
$$

where

$$
\alpha_{ij,t}
=
\frac{
\exp(b^{comm}_{ij,t})
}{
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{N}^{comm}_{i,t}}
\exp(b^{comm}_{ik,t})
}.
$$

This formulation enables the policy to account for neighboring decision dependencies without exposing the full pack state to every decentralized actor.

---

#### 3.4.6.6 Communication Graph and Centralized Critic

Although the decentralized actors may use local observations and communication messages, the centralized critic can exploit the full communication graph.

The centralized critic is defined as

$$
V_{\phi}
=
V_{\phi}
\left(
\mathbf{H}_t,
\mathbf{B}^{comm}_t,
\mathbf{W}_t,
\mathbf{C}_t
\right),
$$

where $\mathbf{H}_t$ is the agent feature matrix, $\mathbf{B}^{comm}_t$ is the communication weight matrix, $\mathbf{W}_t$ is the Battery Energy Interaction Graph weight matrix, and $\mathbf{C}_t$ is the Conflict Graph matrix.

In a simpler implementation, the critic receives the flattened physical pack state:

$$
s^{critic}_t
=
[
\mathbf{SOC}_t,
\mathbf{V}_t,
\mathbf{T}_t,
\mathbf{SOH}_t
].
$$

However, the graph-based critic formulation provides a more structured and scalable interpretation:

$$
V_{\phi}(s_t)
\approx
V_{\phi}^{graph}
\left(
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t,
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t,
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t
\right).
$$

This creates a natural path toward future graph neural critic architectures.

---

#### 3.4.6.7 Communication-Aware Joint Policy

The communication-aware decentralized policy is written as

$$
\pi_{\theta}
(a_{i,t}
\mid
\tilde{o}_{i,t})
=
\pi_{\theta}
(a_{i,t}
\mid
o_{i,t},\mathbf{m}_{i,t}).
$$

The joint policy becomes

$$
\pi_{\theta}
(\mathbf{a}_t
\mid
\tilde{\mathbf{o}}_t)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{N}
\pi_{\theta}
(a_{i,t}
\mid
o_{i,t},\mathbf{m}_{i,t}).
$$

This preserves decentralized execution while allowing each agent to condition its decision on relevant local interaction structure.

In practical implementation, the current Safe MAPPO controller may use a simplified form where $\mathbf{m}_{i,t}$ is represented by scheduler-provided candidate features and pack-level summaries. Nevertheless, the Agent Communication Graph formalizes the information structure and enables future graph-based policy extensions.

---

#### 3.4.6.8 Communication Graph as a Coordination Layer

The Agent Communication Graph serves as a coordination layer between individual agents and global optimization.

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph answers:

$$
\text{Which energy transfers are physically meaningful?}
$$

The Conflict Graph answers:

$$
\text{Which transfer decisions are mutually incompatible?}
$$

The Agent Communication Graph answers:

$$
\text{Which agents should coordinate their decisions?}
$$

These three graph structures are complementary.

$$
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
\rightarrow
\text{physical transfer opportunity},
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t
\rightarrow
\text{decision incompatibility},
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t
\rightarrow
\text{agent coordination dependency}.
$$

Together, they provide a complete graph-theoretic foundation for scheduler-conditioned safe MARL.

---

#### 3.4.6.9 Dynamic Communication Topology

Since the battery state changes over time, the communication graph is also dynamic:

$$
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_{t+1}
\ne
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t.
$$

The communication topology evolves according to

$$
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_{t+1}
=
F_{comm}
\left(
\mathcal{G}^{E}_{t+1},
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_{t+1},
\mathbf{X}_{t+1}
\right).
$$

Thus, agent communication depends on the evolving physical and optimization structure of the pack.

A cell that is irrelevant at one time step may become highly connected later if its SOC becomes extreme, its temperature rises, or its routes begin conflicting with other agents.

This adaptive communication topology prevents unnecessary all-to-all communication while preserving coordination where it matters.

---

#### 3.4.6.10 Communication Sparsity

A fully connected communication graph has

$$
N(N-1)
$$

directed communication edges.

For large battery packs, all-to-all communication is inefficient and unnecessary.

Instead, the proposed communication graph is sparse:

$$
|\mathcal{E}^{comm}_t|
\ll
N(N-1).
$$

The average communication degree is

$$
\bar{d}^{comm}_t
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
|\mathcal{N}^{comm}_{i,t}|.
$$

The sparsity ratio is

$$
\rho^{comm}_t
=
\frac{
|\mathcal{E}^{comm}_t|
}{
N(N-1)
}.
$$

Maintaining

$$
\rho^{comm}_t
\ll 1
$$

is important for scalability.

The scheduler-conditioned candidate graph naturally induces sparse communication because each agent only receives a limited number of candidate targets and conflict-related neighbors.

---

#### 3.4.6.11 Graph Attention Interpretation

Although the current implementation uses Safe MAPPO with structured observations, the Agent Communication Graph can be interpreted as an attention graph.

For agent $i$, the attention score assigned to neighbor $j$ may be written as

$$
\alpha_{ij,t}
=
\frac{
\exp
\left(
\text{score}
(
\mathbf{h}_{i,t},
\mathbf{h}_{j,t},
\mathbf{z}_{ij,t}
)
\right)
}{
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{N}^{comm}_{i,t}}
\exp
\left(
\text{score}
(
\mathbf{h}_{i,t},
\mathbf{h}_{k,t},
\mathbf{z}_{ik,t}
)
\right)
}.
$$

A possible score function is

$$
\text{score}
(
\mathbf{h}_{i,t},
\mathbf{h}_{j,t},
\mathbf{z}_{ij,t}
)
=
\mathbf{a}^{\top}
[
\mathbf{W}_h\mathbf{h}_{i,t}
\Vert
\mathbf{W}_h\mathbf{h}_{j,t}
\Vert
\mathbf{W}_e\mathbf{z}_{ij,t}
],
$$

where $\Vert$ denotes concatenation.

The message becomes

$$
\mathbf{m}_{i,t}
=
\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}^{comm}_{i,t}}
\alpha_{ij,t}
\mathbf{W}_h\mathbf{h}_{j,t}.
$$

This interpretation shows that the proposed graph formulation is compatible with future graph attention networks or graph transformers, while the present work remains focused on optimization-guided Safe MAPPO.

---

#### 3.4.6.12 Relation to the Unified Optimization Graph

The Agent Communication Graph is not itself the QUBO graph. Instead, it mediates the relationship between the optimization graph and the MARL policy.

The QUBO construction uses:

$$
\mathbf{c}
\leftarrow
\text{edge weights from }
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t,
$$

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{off}
\leftarrow
\text{conflict couplings from }
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t.
$$

The MARL controller uses:

$$
o_{i,t}
\leftarrow
\text{local state and candidate edge features},
$$

$$
\mathbf{m}_{i,t}
\leftarrow
\text{communication messages from }
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t.
$$

Thus, the full graph hierarchy can be summarized as

$$
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
\rightarrow
\text{route value},
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t
\rightarrow
\text{route incompatibility},
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t
\rightarrow
\text{agent coordination}.
$$

Together, these graphs define both the optimization scheduler and the multi-agent learning architecture.

---

#### 3.4.6.13 Summary

The Agent Communication Graph completes the graph-theoretic formulation of scheduler-conditioned safe MARL. It defines how cell-level agents coordinate their decisions based on energy-transfer opportunities, routing conflicts, and thermal dependencies.

Unlike the Battery Energy Interaction Graph, which models physical transfer potential, and the Conflict Graph, which models incompatibility among candidate routes, the Agent Communication Graph models decision-level coordination among agents.

This graph enables three important capabilities.

First, it provides a principled communication structure for decentralized actors.

Second, it supports scalable centralized training by exposing graph-level coordination patterns to the critic.

Third, it creates a natural extension path toward graph neural policies, graph attention critics, and temporal graph transformers.

Therefore, the Agent Communication Graph serves as the bridge between graph optimization and multi-agent reinforcement learning. It allows the proposed framework to remain both physically grounded and scalable.

### 3.4.7 Graph State Transition and Unified Optimization Graph

#### 3.4.7.1 Motivation

The previous sections introduced three complementary graph structures: the Battery Energy Interaction Graph, the Conflict Graph, and the Agent Communication Graph. Each graph captures a different aspect of active cell balancing.

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph represents physically meaningful energy-transfer opportunities among battery cells. The Conflict Graph represents incompatibilities among candidate route-selection decisions. The Agent Communication Graph represents coordination dependencies among cell-level agents.

Although these graphs serve different purposes, they are not independent. They are generated from the same battery digital twin state and evolve together as the battery pack operates. A balancing action modifies cell SOC, voltage, temperature, and SOH. These physical changes update the energy interaction graph. The updated energy interaction graph changes the candidate routes. The candidate routes update the conflict graph. The changed conflict structure modifies agent communication dependencies. Therefore, active balancing induces a coupled graph-state transition.

This section formalizes this coupled transition and introduces the **Unified Optimization Graph**, which serves as the final graph-theoretic representation used for QUBO construction and scheduler-conditioned Safe MARL.

---

#### 3.4.7.2 Graph State

At time $t$, the complete graph state is defined as

$$
\mathfrak{G}_t
=
\left(
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t,
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t,
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t
\right),
$$

where

$$
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
=
(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t,\mathbf{W}_t)
$$

is the Battery Energy Interaction Graph,

$$
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t
=
(\mathcal{V}^{conf}_t,\mathcal{E}^{conf}_t,\mathbf{C}_t)
$$

is the Conflict Graph, and

$$
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t
=
(\mathcal{V}^{agent},\mathcal{E}^{comm}_t,\mathbf{B}^{comm}_t)
$$

is the Agent Communication Graph.

The graph state is generated from the digital twin state:

$$
\mathfrak{G}_t
=
\mathcal{F}_{graph}(s_t).
$$

This mapping consists of three stages:

$$
s_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t.
$$

The Battery Energy Interaction Graph is derived directly from physical variables. The Conflict Graph is derived from candidate route interactions. The Agent Communication Graph is derived from both physical interaction and decision dependency.

---

#### 3.4.7.3 Graph-State Transition

Given an executed balancing edge set

$$
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t,
$$

the battery digital twin updates the physical state:

$$
s_{t+1}
=
f_{\mathcal{D}}
\left(
s_t,
I^{load}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t,
\Theta
\right).
$$

The graph state is then updated as

$$
\mathfrak{G}_{t+1}
=
\mathcal{F}_{graph}(s_{t+1}).
$$

Combining these two equations gives

$$
\mathfrak{G}_{t+1}
=
\mathcal{F}_{graph}
\left(
f_{\mathcal{D}}
\left(
s_t,
I^{load}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t,
\Theta
\right)
\right).
$$

Since

$$
\mathfrak{G}_t
=
\mathcal{F}_{graph}(s_t),
$$

the graph-state transition may be written abstractly as

$$
\mathfrak{G}_{t+1}
=
\mathcal{T}_{G}
\left(
\mathfrak{G}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t,
I^{load}_t,
\Theta
\right).
$$

This equation shows that graph evolution is not arbitrary. It is induced by physical battery dynamics and balancing decisions.

---

#### 3.4.7.4 Coupled Graph Update Sequence

The coupled graph update proceeds in the following order.

First, node features are updated by the digital twin:

$$
\mathbf{X}_{t+1}
=
F_X
\left(
\mathbf{X}_t,
I^{load}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t,
\Theta
\right).
$$

Second, feasible directed energy-transfer edges are regenerated:

$$
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_{t+1}
=
F_E
\left(
\mathbf{X}_{t+1}
\right).
$$

Third, edge weights are recomputed:

$$
\mathbf{W}_{t+1}
=
F_W
\left(
\mathbf{X}_{t+1},
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_{t+1}
\right).
$$

Fourth, candidate route variables are defined:

$$
\mathbf{x}_{t+1}
=
[
x_{1,t+1},
x_{2,t+1},
\dots,
x_{M_{t+1},t+1}
]^{\top}.
$$

Fifth, the Conflict Graph is reconstructed:

$$
\mathbf{C}_{t+1}
=
F_C
\left(
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_{t+1}
\right).
$$

Sixth, the Agent Communication Graph is updated:

$$
\mathbf{B}^{comm}_{t+1}
=
F_{comm}
\left(
\mathcal{G}^{E}_{t+1},
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_{t+1},
\mathbf{X}_{t+1}
\right).
$$

Thus, the complete graph update chain is

$$
\mathbf{X}_{t+1}
\rightarrow
\mathcal{E}^{cand}_{t+1}
\rightarrow
\mathbf{W}_{t+1}
\rightarrow
\mathbf{C}_{t+1}
\rightarrow
\mathbf{B}^{comm}_{t+1}.
$$

---

#### 3.4.7.5 Unified Optimization Graph

The Unified Optimization Graph is defined as

$$
\mathcal{G}^{U}_t
=
\left(
\mathcal{V}^{opt}_t,
\mathcal{E}^{opt}_t,
\mathbf{q}_t,
\mathbf{Q}^{int}_t
\right),
$$

where

$$
\mathcal{V}^{opt}_t
=
\{
x_1,x_2,\dots,x_M
\}
$$

is the set of binary route-selection variables,

$$
\mathcal{E}^{opt}_t
$$

is the set of interactions among these variables,

$$
\mathbf{q}_t
$$

is the linear edge-cost vector derived from the Battery Energy Interaction Graph, and

$$
\mathbf{Q}^{int}_t
$$

is the quadratic interaction matrix derived from the Conflict Graph.

For each candidate route variable $x_m$, the linear coefficient is

$$
q_{m,t}
=
c_{m,t}
=
-w_{m,t}.
$$

For each pair of route variables $(x_m,x_n)$, the quadratic coefficient is

$$
Q^{int}_{mn,t}
=
C_{mn,t}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathcal{G}^{U}_t
$$

is an optimization-domain graph whose nodes are binary route-selection variables and whose weighted edges represent quadratic couplings.

---

#### 3.4.7.6 From Graph State to QUBO Matrix

The Unified Optimization Graph directly induces a QUBO matrix.

Let

$$
\mathbf{x}_t
=
[x_{1,t},x_{2,t},\dots,x_{M,t}]^{\top}
$$

be the binary decision vector.

The energy function is

$$
E_t(\mathbf{x}_t)
=
\sum_{m=1}^{M}
q_{m,t}x_{m,t}
+
\sum_{m<n}
Q^{int}_{mn,t}x_{m,t}x_{n,t}.
$$

This can be written compactly as

$$
E_t(\mathbf{x}_t)
=
\mathbf{x}_t^{\top}
\mathbf{Q}_t
\mathbf{x}_t.
$$

The QUBO matrix is defined by

$$
Q_{mm,t}
=
q_{m,t},
$$

and

$$
Q_{mn,t}
=
Q^{int}_{mn,t},
\quad
m\ne n.
$$

Thus,

$$
\mathbf{Q}_t
=
\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{q}_t)
+
\mathbf{Q}^{int}_t.
$$

This equation is central to the proposed framework. It shows that the QUBO matrix is not manually constructed from arbitrary penalties. Rather, it is derived from the unified graph representation:

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf{Q}_t
=
\operatorname{diag}
\left(
-\mathbf{w}_t
\right)
+
\mathbf{C}_t
}
$$

where $\mathbf{w}_t$ comes from the Battery Energy Interaction Graph and $\mathbf{C}_t$ comes from the Conflict Graph.

---

#### 3.4.7.7 Unified Graph Hierarchy

The complete graph hierarchy is summarized as follows:

$$
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
\rightarrow
\mathbf{w}_t
\rightarrow
\operatorname{diag}(-\mathbf{w}_t),
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t
\rightarrow
\mathbf{C}_t,
$$

$$
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t
\rightarrow
\text{MARL coordination structure}.
$$

The QUBO scheduler uses

$$
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
\quad
\text{and}
\quad
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t,
$$

while the Safe MARL controller uses

$$
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t,
\quad
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t,
\quad
\text{and}
\quad
\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t.
$$

Therefore, the graph hierarchy serves both optimization and learning.

---

#### 3.4.7.8 Scheduler View

From the scheduler perspective, the graph-state-to-QUBO mapping is

$$
s_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{G}^{E}_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{G}^{conf}_t
\rightarrow
\mathbf{Q}_t
\rightarrow
\mathbf{x}^{*}_t.
$$

The scheduler solves

$$
\mathbf{x}^{*}_t
=
\arg\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{M}}
\mathbf{x}^{\top}
\mathbf{Q}_t
\mathbf{x}.
$$

The selected schedule is

$$
\mathcal{E}^{sched}_t
=
\{
e_m
\mid
x^{*}_{m,t}=1
\}.
$$

This schedule is not necessarily the final executed action. Instead, it provides a structured candidate set or prior for the Safe MARL controller.

---

#### 3.4.7.9 MARL View

From the Safe MARL perspective, the graph hierarchy defines the agent observation and coordination structure.

Each agent observes:

$$
o_{i,t}
=
[
\mathbf{x}_{i,t},
\mathbf{g}_t,
\Phi_{i,t},
\mathbf{m}_{i,t}
],
$$

where

$$
\Phi_{i,t}
$$

is derived from candidate edge features in $\mathcal{G}^{E}_t$, and

$$
\mathbf{m}_{i,t}
$$

is derived from the Agent Communication Graph.

The policy is

$$
a_{i,t}
\sim
\pi_{\theta}
(a_{i,t}
\mid
o_{i,t}).
$$

The joint policy is

$$
\pi_{\theta}
(\mathbf{a}_t
\mid
\mathbf{o}_t)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{N}
\pi_{\theta}
(a_{i,t}
\mid
o_{i,t}).
$$

The raw action is mapped back into balancing routes:

$$
\mathbf{a}_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{E}^{raw}_t.
$$

Then conflict resolution and safety projection are applied:

$$
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t
=
\mathcal{P}
\left(
\mathcal{R}
\left(
\mathcal{E}^{raw}_t
\right)
\right).
$$

Thus, the MARL controller operates on the same graph structure as the scheduler but uses it for adaptive sequential decision-making rather than one-step combinatorial optimization.

---

#### 3.4.7.10 Closed-Loop Graph-Control Dynamics

The complete closed-loop graph-control system is written as

$$
s_t
\rightarrow
\mathfrak{G}_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{G}^{U}_t
\rightarrow
\mathbf{Q}_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{E}^{sched}_t
\rightarrow
\mathbf{a}^{raw}_t
\rightarrow
\mathcal{E}^{bal}_t
\rightarrow
s_{t+1}
\rightarrow
\mathfrak{G}_{t+1}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
s_{t+1}
=
f_{\mathcal{D}}
\left(
s_t,
I^{load}_t,
\mathcal{P}
\left[
\mathcal{R}
\left(
\pi_{\theta}
(
\mathcal{S}_{Q}
(
\mathfrak{G}_t
)
)
\right)
\right],
\Theta
\right).
$$

This equation expresses the entire proposed framework in one closed-loop form.

The physical battery state generates a graph. The graph generates an optimization problem. The optimization problem generates structured candidates. The MARL controller selects adaptive actions. The safety layer projects actions into the feasible set. The digital twin updates the physical state. The graph is then regenerated.

---

#### 3.4.7.11 Why the Unified Graph Matters

The Unified Optimization Graph provides three major benefits.

First, it makes QUBO construction interpretable. The diagonal terms are derived from route-level physical desirability, while the off-diagonal terms are derived from explicit route conflicts.

Second, it separates physical modeling from optimization structure. Battery physics enters through edge weights, while hardware and interaction constraints enter through conflict couplings.

Third, it provides a common interface between classical optimization, quantum-compatible optimization, and safe multi-agent reinforcement learning.

This is especially important because the proposed framework does not treat QUBO, Ising, and MARL as disconnected modules. Instead, all three are derived from the same evolving graph state.

---

#### 3.4.7.12 Computational Structure

Let $M_t$ denote the number of candidate routes at time $t$. The QUBO matrix has dimension

$$
M_t\times M_t.
$$

The cost of dense matrix storage is

$$
O(M_t^2).
$$

However, the conflict matrix is usually sparse because most route pairs do not conflict. Therefore, sparse storage requires only

$$
O(|\mathcal{E}^{conf}_t|)
$$

memory.

The number of binary variables is determined by candidate routes:

$$
M_t
=
|\mathcal{E}^{cand}_t|.
$$

Since the scheduler restricts each agent to at most $K$ candidate targets,

$$
M_t
\le
NK.
$$

Thus, instead of scaling as

$$
O(N^2),
$$

the candidate variable count scales approximately as

$$
O(NK),
$$

where $K\ll N$.

This is crucial for large-scale battery packs.

---

#### 3.4.7.13 Dynamic QUBO Sequence

Because the graph changes over time, the QUBO matrix also changes over time:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_0,
\mathbf{Q}_1,
\dots,
\mathbf{Q}_T.
$$

Thus, active cell balancing is not a single static QUBO problem. It is a sequence of state-dependent QUBO problems:

$$
\mathbf{x}^{*}_t
=
\arg\min_{\mathbf{x}_t}
\mathbf{x}_t^{\top}
\mathbf{Q}_t
\mathbf{x}_t,
\quad
t=0,\dots,T.
$$

This temporal QUBO sequence is coupled through battery dynamics:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{t+1}
=
F_Q
\left(
\mathbf{Q}_t,
\mathbf{x}_t,
I^{load}_t,
\Theta
\right).
$$

The Safe MARL controller learns how to interact with this evolving QUBO-conditioned decision landscape.

---

#### 3.4.7.14 Bridge to Ising and Hamiltonian Formulation

The Unified Optimization Graph prepares the problem for Ising transformation.

Given the QUBO objective

$$
E(\mathbf{x})
=
\mathbf{x}^{\top}
\mathbf{Q}
\mathbf{x},
$$

with

$$
x_i\in\{0,1\},
$$

the binary variables are converted to spin variables:

$$
x_i
=
\frac{1+z_i}{2},
\quad
z_i\in\{-1,+1\}.
$$

Therefore, the same graph-derived QUBO can be transformed into an Ising energy:

$$
E(\mathbf{z})
=
\sum_i h_i z_i
+
\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}z_i z_j
+
C.
$$

The Ising couplings

$$
J_{ij}
$$

are directly related to the graph-derived quadratic terms.

Thus, the Conflict Graph becomes the physical origin of the Ising coupling structure.

This observation is central to the quantum-compatible interpretation of the proposed scheduler.

---

#### 3.4.7.15 Summary

This section introduced the Graph State Transition and Unified Optimization Graph formulation. The proposed framework does not treat battery states, optimization variables, and multi-agent policies as independent entities. Instead, it defines a coupled graph-state system in which physical battery dynamics generate evolving graph structures, and those graph structures generate both optimization problems and policy observations.

The key relation is

$$
\mathbf{Q}_t
=
\operatorname{diag}
(-\mathbf{w}_t)
+
\mathbf{C}_t.
$$

This equation summarizes the transition from battery physics to QUBO optimization:

- $\mathbf{w}_t$ originates from the Battery Energy Interaction Graph;
- $\mathbf{C}_t$ originates from the Conflict Graph;
- $\mathbf{Q}_t$ defines the quantum-compatible optimization problem;
- $\mathcal{G}^{comm}_t$ defines the coordination structure for Safe MARL.

The Unified Optimization Graph therefore completes the graph-theoretic bridge from digital twin dynamics to QUBO, Ising Hamiltonian construction, and scheduler-conditioned safe multi-agent reinforcement learning.
